en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui.
Part Two: Resolving the Doubt that the Knots are of the Same Substance. Section One: Ānanda’s Request. Subsection One:
Relating His Continued Confusion.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Although the Tathāgata has explained this second gateway of meaning, when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie knots, if they do not know the origin from which the knot was tied, I believe such people will ultimately be unable to untie it.”

Previously, there was doubt regarding the identity or difference between cause and effect; now, there is doubt regarding the binding and liberation of the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Therefore, this is called the second thematic gate.

Although the causes for the arising of the faculties were extensively demonstrated previously, it was not specifically pointed out where the binding occurs, and the meaning of binding and liberation has not yet been clarified. Desiring to provide a precise exposition so that it may be clearly understood, he cites the metaphors previously raised by the Buddha to illustrate his own delusion.
“World-Honored One!

It is the same for me and the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training: from the beginningless past, we have been born and extinguished together with various forms of ignorance. Although we have attained such roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called ‘those who have left home,’ we remain like those suffering from a quotidian malaria.”

"All ignorance" (*sarvāvidyā*) refers to the ignorance of the entire realm (*dhātu*), which comprehensively subsumes all two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*)—namely, those of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, it is called "all.

Beginning with the delusion regarding the True [Suchness], it follows sentient beings throughout their arising and ceasing without ever departing from them; thus, as stated in the preceding passage, "In conjunction they falsely arise; in conjunction they falsely die," it is said that they "perish together and arise together."

Although those in the first fruit who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) have not yet severed their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are already said to have destroyed the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and attained realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). However, because they have not at all destroyed the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) still persists, it is said that they are "still separated by a daily malaria."
2. Requesting Instruction on Bondage and Liberation:
"I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will take pity on those submerged in suffering. Today, how is it that body and mind constitute bondage?
From what does liberation arise?"
"May it also cause sentient beings suffering in future kalpas to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the great assembly, raining down tears with uplifted sincerity as he awaited the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
That we have been unable to transcend birth and death since beginningless time is due to our fetters.
Now that we await their release to become unimpeded and unbound, we cannot achieve awakening through mere earnestness alone; therefore, we shed tears and seek your instruction.
II. The Tathāgata’s Extensive Exposition, in five parts:
1. The World-Honored One’s Touching of the Crown of the Head.

At that time, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training, and also for the sake of all future sentient beings—to serve as the cause for transcending the world and to act as eyes for the future—the World-Honored One used his hand, which was like Jambūnada gold with purple light, to touch the crown of Ānanda’s head.

The crown of the head is the aggregate of all faculties, and the hand is the essential means for untying knots; by rubbing it, one awakens and stirs them so that liberation may be expected, and by stroking it, one comforts and reassures them so that they may know the profound meaning.
2. The Buddhas Emit Light.

At that moment, the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways. From the crowns of the heads of all the Tathāgatas dwelling in those worlds, rays of precious light issued forth. Simultaneously, these lights came from those worlds to the Jeta Grove and descended upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head; the great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
The ground of abiding ignorance serves as the six sense organs; they vibrate and are restless, and it is through this that the knots are untied.
The radiant light of all Buddhas flows and pours over the crown of a single Buddha, symbolizing the non-obstruction between the one and the many, and the equality of self and others.
In the following text, the Buddhas provide the indication while this Buddha provides the explanation; they speak in unison and realize in concert, with no divergent paths.
Question:

From the beginning of this sutra up to this point, light has been emitted four times. Why is it that only in this present passage do all the Buddhas emit light together and furthermore speak in unison? This is what makes it particularly extraordinary.
Answer:

First, the teaching is expounded to refute heterodoxy; next, it is used to discern the false and reveal the principle; next, it is used to stabilize insight and generate wisdom; and now, it is for entering contemplation and accomplishing practice.
In the preceding three sections, understanding was developed based on the teachings, yet obstacles had not yet been removed;

now, with the completion of the contemplation in this text, delusions are shattered and ignorance is directly shaken, as one enters the principle of the Dharma-realm. Therefore, all Buddhas emit light to collectively demonstrate that the substance of the untying of knots has no dual source.

Therefore, we know that teaching the Dharma to refute the heterodox, revealing the true while discerning the false, and establishing faith to achieve understanding, are all for the purpose of perfecting practice and attaining realization today; they are no trivial matters, which is why they differ from the preceding text.
3. The Unified Declaration on the Roots of Bondage.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly together heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, speaking with one voice and in unison, saying to Ānanda:
"Excellent, Ānanda!"
If you wish to recognize the co-nascent ignorance that causes you to revolve in birth and death as its root, it is none other than your six sense faculties; there is nothing else.

Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that enables you to swiftly realize peace, bliss, liberation, and the wondrous, eternal tranquility, it is likewise your six sense faculties and nothing else.

When the clarity of awareness first arose, the duality of subject and object was falsely produced; once the nature of profound stillness was divided, the six sense organs became distinct. As the organs and their objects coincided, the nature of karma immediately arose, leading to endless cycles of transmigration and long-term bondage to birth and death. Thus, these six sense organs are the source of the fetters of birth and death.

In a single thought-moment, there is no-thought; both subject and object vanish entirely. The sense organs, their objects, and the consciousnesses fall away simultaneously. There is no truth to be attained and no delusion to be removed. The nature of awakening is perfectly luminous and the Dharma-eye is pure; thus, these six sense faculties become the source of sovereign liberation, peace, bliss, and wondrous permanence.

It is like ice and water, which shift according to the movement of vapor; though their forms change, their moist nature remains constant. That the states of freezing and melting share the same underlying principle is likewise so.
Fourth, Ānanda requests again.
Although Ānanda had heard such a Dharma-sound, his mind was still not yet clear. He bowed his head to the Buddha and said:
"How can it be that both my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal state of peace and bliss are identical to these six faculties, and nothing else?"

"The root of both defilement and purity consists solely in these six faculties; there is no other dharma apart from them. Upon these, one gives rise to views and undergoes the cycle of birth and death; upon these, one forgets emotions and attains the eternal bliss of nirvana."
If attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not been shattered, who can penetrate and clarify [the truth]?
Therefore, he inquired again, desiring an exposition.
Fifth, the Buddha’s explanation for the sake of clarification, in two parts:
I. The prose section, in two parts:
A. The dual introduction.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual; the nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky.
The three—faculties, objects, and consciousness—have no distinct essential natures; they are but the single true awakening, and thus are said to share the same source.

When clinging views are not extinguished, one falsely gives rise to grasping and attachment, forcibly distinguishing between defilement and purity, and recklessly calculating the nature of body and mind; from beginning to end, these undergo moment-to-moment arising and ceasing, and are therefore said to be "bondage."

Having realized both the characterized and the uncharacterized, discrimination does not arise; subject and object are stilled, and thoughts and perceptions are exhausted into emptiness. When not a single dharma is grasped, the one true reality manifests; mind and empty space are equal and without distinction—therefore, this is called liberation.

Regarding the statement that "the nature of consciousness is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky": it refers to the mutual reflection between the faculties and objects mentioned above. Previously, it was said that the faculties and objects reflect this nature of consciousness; now, it is said that the nature of consciousness reflects the preceding faculties and objects. Thus, these three share a common source and are equally illusory. Therefore, the preceding text states: "The seer, the conditions for seeing, and the perceived characteristics are like flowers in the sky."
"This very nature of consciousness is illusory.
Furthermore, it says, "This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi.
This refers to the fact that the sense faculties and their objects share a common source.
II. A dual explanation, in two parts:
A. A general manifestation of the absence of intrinsic nature. "Ānanda!..."
"Knowledge is triggered by objects, and appearances arise because of the sense organs; appearance and perception lack inherent nature, being like the intertwined stalks of a reed.
Grasping at objects forms the organs, and in opposition to the organs, appearances exist; thus, the organ and its object are established, and deluded consciousness arises.

The deluded consciousness is able to transform into the two dharmas of sense organs and objects; therefore, the organs, objects, and consciousnesses depend upon one another, such that each is empty of intrinsic substance yet each is established, resembling bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
2. Specific Explanation of Bondage and Liberation:
"Therefore, if you now establish cognition upon your knowledge and vision, this is the very root of ignorance;
if your knowledge and vision are free from seeing, this is precisely Nirvana—taintless, truly pure. How could any other thing be admitted within this?"
Ānanda asked again:
"Why is it that my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal bliss are both identical to these six faculties, and nothing else?"

Therefore, the Buddha first demonstrated that the three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—are solely illusory and share a single source of nature; that delusion and bondage, as well as liberation, are truly not different paths. By this, he specifically provides a detailed answer to ensure there is no doubt, so that through understanding one may cultivate contemplation, and the wondrous fruit may be hoped for.
The phrase "knowing this" is a brief mention of two of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The establishment of "knowledge" further abbreviates the character for "seeing," which is implicitly present in the subsequent text.

The intended meaning is that if, regarding the three matters of the six sense faculties, one fails to understand their lack of intrinsic nature and instead establishes them as truly existent, giving rise to pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), then delusion and karma will arise; one will thus voluntarily take up saṃsāra and unjustly enter the various realms of existence (*gati*). In this way, the six sense faculties constitute the root of the bonds of ignorance and birth-and-death.

If one, within this very state, realizes the truth and penetrates the delusion, so that grasping does not arise and false cognition, views, and awareness vanish into a profound stillness and silence, leaving only the perfectly accomplished, pure, and precious awakening—then the six sense faculties are themselves the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvana; what further thing could there be to call a different cause?
Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "If one perceives that all marks are non-marks, one then perceives the Tathāgata.
As stated above: "This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi."
This is precisely the correct refutation of the dharma-attachment of ignorance, which accomplishes the gate of perfect penetration.
Second, the verse commentary, in two parts:
first, the heading.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"In general discussion, there are four types of verses:
first, the *anuṣṭubh* verse; regardless of whether it is in prose or verse, if it consists of thirty-two syllables, it constitutes one verse."

The second is called *gāthā*, which here is translated as "recited verse" (*fèngsòng*) or "direct verse" (*zhí sòng*); this refers to the teaching of the Dharma by means of stanzas, rather than verses that recapitulate prose.
The third is called *geya*, which here is translated as "verses in response" (*yìngsòng*).

The fourth is called *gāthodāna*, which here is translated as "verses of gathered giving" (*jísī sòng*); this refers to the condensation of many meanings into few words for the purpose of bestowing them upon others for recitation and retention.
For what purpose are many verses established in the sūtras?
Briefly, there are eight reasons:
first, because a few words encompass many meanings; [and so forth].
Second, because eulogies are mostly composed in verse;
third, because of the need for repeated explanation for those of dull faculties;
and fourth, for the sake of those who arrive later.
Fifth, because it accords with their inclinations;
sixth, because it is easy to uphold;
seventh, because it further elucidates what was previously taught.

Because eight [factors] were not previously mentioned in the prose section, they are now subsumed within the second and third of the four previously mentioned; among the eight intentions, there are strictly three and seven, while the second, fifth, and eighth are included as well.
Furthermore, when comparing the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*), there are five pairs of corresponding patterns:

namely, presence and absence, expansion and abbreviation, separation and combination, priority and posteriority, and concealment and manifestation; these shall be understood in detail from the text itself.

These nine lines of verse consist of a mixture of *geya* (verses corresponding to prose) and *geya* (rhymed verses), linked like a chain that arises and recurs, mutually generating one another. Their general purport is to destroy the ignorance of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), causing the gates of contemplation to become clear and pure, so that through practice one may realize and enter the single true Dharma-realm (*ekasatyadharmadhātu*).
II. The Main Verses, in six parts:
First, two verses stating the fundamental tenet and refuting attachments, in two sections: A.

Refutation by means of inference: "The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty, because they arise dependently, like illusions; unconditioned phenomena have no arising or ceasing, and are unreal like flowers in the sky."

This passage specifically refutes the dharma-attachment of ignorance, which clings to both the conditioned and the unconditioned as having substantial reality; all such views are delusions regarding true nature.
Since the single true Dharma-realm is fundamentally not a matter of opposition, this dual refutation is precisely the cause for unraveling the knots.

Regarding these four propositions, the first two refute the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the latter two refute the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); only when these two are not established is the meaning of the single characteristic of the *dharmadhātu* revealed.

Regarding the statement "the true nature (tathatā) is empty of the conditioned," the phrase "true nature" precisely marks the central thesis and distinguishes the dharma; it extends through the second formal inference (pramāṇa) below. This refers to the one true Middle Way, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). One should formulate the inference as follows:
The conditioned is originally empty and non-existent in its true nature because it arises from conditions, just like a magical illusion;
The unconditioned is fundamentally unreal in its true nature because it is devoid of arising and ceasing, just like flowers in the sky.

Because these two means of valid cognition and three members are complete, clearly distinguished, and free from all faults, they are adopted as well-established in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (*Pal-zhen lun*).
In the second measure, the reason is stated first and the thesis last; this follows the translator’s stylistic convenience and incurs no loss of meaning.

The truth revealed by this principle is that of the single, true equality, which is devoid of all dualistic oppositions. Whether it be truth or falsehood, defilement or purity, birth-and-death or nirvana, ordinary beings or Buddhas—all are like flowers in the sky, arising and ceasing in confusion. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "All worlds, mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana, are all but the delusory, inverted appearances of flowers."

Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent; now, since there is no dependence, there is likewise no phenomenon to be established."

This reveals that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all marks are transcended; the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases, whereby ignorance and the clinging to dharmas are here exhausted.
2. Refutation by Exposing Faults through Contrast:
"To speak of the false as manifesting the various truths makes both the false and the true equally false; since it is neither true nor not-true, how can there be a seer and that which is seen?"
The first two phrases reiterate the preceding fault because conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are mutually dependent.
They also serve to refute attachment; for if true nature were an existent entity, it would be no different from the false.
A deluded person might argue:

"Although within the true nature (tathatā) both the conditioned and the unconditioned are absent, this true nature must nonetheless be something that can be attained; it is what the Buddha realized, and because it is free from all falsehood and delusion, it is called 'true'."
The nature of these phenomena must ultimately exist.
Therefore, this refutation states:

if one claims that there is a true nature manifested apart from the delusory, it is identical to delusory phenomena and is likewise delusory, because it is an object of perception for pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

The reality that transcends delusion is revealed precisely because of delusion; as the preceding text states: "When the bodhicitta arises, the mind of arising and ceasing is extinguished—this too is arising and ceasing.

The *Awakening of Faith* likewise says: "That which is called True Suchness (tathatā) is also without marks; it is the ultimate limit of verbal expression, wherein words are used to dispel words. This essence of True Suchness cannot be dispelled, for all phenomena are entirely true; nor can anything be established, for all phenomena are identical with Suchness."
"One should know that all dharmas are ineffable and inconceivable; therefore, they are called *tathatā* (suchness).
One should understand that if there were any true nature to be attained, it would all be delusion; hence it is said that "delusion and truth are equally two forms of delusion."

The first phrase follows up on what was previously negated: since there is neither "true" nor "not true," that which is "not true" is precisely the delusory. How much more so, then, does this refute the attachment to the false as expressed in the latter two phrases?

The next line provides the formal analogy: how could there still exist that which sees and that which is seen? Both the sense organ and consciousness are termed "seeing," while that which is seen is the object.

This constitutes a comprehensive refutation of both the true and the deluded minds; when all dualistic phenomena are found to be non-existent, it is only then called the manifestation of the pure Dharma-realm, the single truth of equality.
These two preceding verses precisely eulogize the fact that the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share a common source.
Since the fundamental nature of the original source is neither true nor false, how could the existence of the organs, objects, and consciousness be maintained?
Therefore, the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses share this same single source.
Second, the two verses conclude that their union and dissolution are of the same essence:
"In the interim there is no real nature; therefore, they are like intertwined reeds."
The preceding verse stated that the faculties and their objects arise through mutual conditioning; yet their characteristics and their seeing lack inherent nature, being like intertwined reeds.
"Bondage and liberation share the same cause; for the sage and the ordinary person, there are no two paths."
The preceding verse clarifies that bondage and liberation are non-dual.
Ordinary beings of the six realms are bound by karma and afflictions and lack self-mastery; therefore, they are called "bound.
The worthy and noble ones of the Three Vehicles have severed afflictions and realized the principle, and thus do not follow the constraints of karma; therefore, they are called "liberated."
This is entirely due to the delusion or enlightenment of the six sense faculties; there is no other divergence, and thus there are not two paths.
"Observe the nature within this intersection: it is neither empty nor existent."

Since there is no intrinsic nature within the interdependent arising of phenomena, what is there to eliminate from existence so that non-existence might further persist? This is because within the single nature of reality, there are no opposing counterparts.
Master Zhao said:
"If existence does not exist, then non-existence is likewise non-existent."
This precisely reveals the Middle Way between the faculties and their objects, and it also expresses the principle that the source of the faculties and objects is one and the same.
"When obscured by delusion, there is ignorance; when illumination is revealed, there is liberation."
This refers to the preceding verse concerning "establishing knowledge based on what is known and seen.
To take delusion as the root and grasp at objects, failing to realize that their nature is empty and falsely perceiving them as existent, is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).

Realizing that nature is devoid of inherent nature, truth and delusion are one and the same; since the triad of faculties, objects, and consciousness cannot act as fetters, it is called liberation—this is precisely nirvana, the untainted, true purity.
3. One verse introduces the subsequent text:
"The sequence for untying the knots is such that when the six are untied, even the one perishes.
This raises the doubt as to how the six are untied and the one subsequently perishes.

Regarding the sequence of causes, the subsequent text states: "This faculty first attains understanding and initially realizes the emptiness of persons; as the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation from dharmas.

Once liberated from dharmas, both [person and dharma] are empty and do not arise; this is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the forbearance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) from samādhi."

Regarding "even 'one' perishes," the subsequent text states: "If the Tathāgata were today to completely release [the bonds], and if the knots did not arise, then there would be neither 'this' nor 'that'; they would not even be called 'one,' so how could 'six' be established?"
"By selecting the faculty of the ear as the perfect penetration, one enters the stream and achieves true enlightenment.

This introduces the subsequent section on the cultivation and realization of perfect penetration, specifically taking Avalokiteśvara’s entry into *samādhi* through the gateway of the auditory faculty.
Those selected by Mañjuśrī are capable of entering the stream toward perfect enlightenment alongside Ānanda and the people of this world.
Fourth, one verse on the habitual tendencies of ignorance:
"The subtle *ālayavijñāna* has its habitual tendencies forming a violent torrent."
"Ādāna" means "to grasp and maintain"; it refers to the eighth consciousness, for it is able to grasp and maintain the seeds and give rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
Among the many names for the eighth consciousness, this name is the most comprehensive; it denotes the stage of continuous grasping and maintenance throughout the three states [of existence].

The seeds of the perfuming of ignorance are not severed, flowing incessantly like a torrential stream; these subtle objects of perception can be known only by a Buddha. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The consciousnesses arising from the perfuming of ignorance cannot be known by ordinary beings, nor can they be realized through the wisdom of the two vehicles."

This means that based on a bodhisattva’s initial cultivation of right faith and the arousal of the mind of enlightenment, if they realize the dharmakāya, they attain a partial knowledge; even up to the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva, one cannot know it exhaustively—it is only the Buddha who fully comprehends it.
"I fear that [discriminating between] the real and the unreal may lead to delusion; therefore, I have never openly expounded this.

This means that the substance of this consciousness cannot be established as purely real alone, nor can it be formed as purely false alone; it is only through the union of the real and the false that it functions.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is the union of the unborn and undying with the arising and ceasing, being neither identical nor different, is called the ālayavijñāna.
If one were to say that this is identical to the True [Nature], how could the habitual tendencies of delusion ever be exhausted?
Ordinary beings and non-Buddhists give rise to the view of eternalism, clinging to it as a true self.
If one were to say that this is false, they fear it would lead to the negation of existence as annihilationism, because the characteristic of truth does not perish.
For this reason, the eighth consciousness is not mentioned in the Śrāvaka-piṭaka or in the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna.

The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The ādānavijñāna is extremely subtle; all seeds form a turbulent stream. I do not reveal it to ordinary people and fools, fearing that they might conceptually grasp it as a self."

This intends to clarify that the sixfold fetters of the preceding passage—the three factors of faculty, object, and consciousness—are all produced through the transformation of the perfuming of this consciousness. Whether grasping at the real or the unreal, or perceiving existence or emptiness, these are solely the shadows of this consciousness; even the Buddha-bodies perceived by Bodhisattvas up to the tenth stage are seen upon the level of karmic consciousness.
If a Buddha-Tathāgata has already transcended the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and is devoid of the perception of self and other, as described in the *Awakening of Faith*,
this precisely demonstrates that he has already transcended innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*).
5. One verse and one line dispel the notions of illusion and non-illusion:
"The self-mind grasps the self-mind; that which is not illusory becomes an illusory phenomenon.
All phenomena are transformations of consciousness alone; therefore, they are all the self-mind.

The first six consciousnesses lack clarity; they perceive objects as coming from the outside, grasping them and making distinctions. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The three realms are false and illusory, produced solely by the mind."

"When the mind is detached, the six sensory realms cease to exist; for all phenomena arise from the mind through the production of deluded thoughts. All discrimination is simply the discrimination of one's own mind; therefore, it is said that 'the self-mind grasps the self-mind.'"

If one considers that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks, then fundamentally there have never been worlds or sentient beings; therefore, it is said to be "not illusory.

Yet, due to the sudden arising of deluded views, the manifestation of the appearance of cognitive clarity occurs, the four great elements become differentiated, and the sense organs and their objects are fully established; therefore, it is said that "illusory dharmas are formed."
As for what is called "illusion," it is because each and every phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature.
"There is nothing that is not taken up as non-illusion; since even non-illusion does not arise, how could illusory phenomena be established?"
When discrimination does not arise and the boundaries of the past and future are severed, even reality itself cannot be discerned; how then could delusion be established?

Therefore, within the eternally true nature, one seeks in vain for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, finding nothing at all. This is the state of the single mark of equality, where both delusion and enlightenment have utterly vanished, and birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday.
Therefore, Master Sengzhao said:
"He who does not rely on non-existence to contemplate dharmas may be said to perceive the true mark of dharmas.
Sixth, one verse with three lines praises the Dharma to inspire joy.
"This is called the 'Sublime Lotus.
This contemplation of the nature of equality can shatter ignorance and open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

This nature of knowledge and vision is eternally true amidst delusion and remains unstained within defilement; now it is manifested and revealed, like a flower blooming above the water, and thus serves as a metaphor."

“Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening”: Ignorance is firm and solid, most difficult to destroy; yet with a single thought it can be shattered by the power of the Vajra-samādhi. This samādhi is supreme, beyond which nothing excels; one attains mastery over all dharmas and is thus worthy of being cherished as a treasure. Like a maṇi jewel that produces whatever is desired at will, this unsurpassed fruit of awakening is called the King-Jewel Awakening.

"When the samādhi of 'illusion-like' manifests before one's vision," one realizes that all phenomena are like illusory transformations; they are like various forms and images appearing in a clear mirror, where the substance of each individual form and image cannot be apprehended, yet they are identical to the clarity of the mirror—neither identical to it nor separate from it.
Samādhi is called "right reception," meaning that one does not receive any further sensations.

"A snap of the fingers transcends the stage of no-more-learning" (aśaikṣa) reveals that one can swiftly reach Great Enlightenment; thus, when not a single thought arises, one is immediately named a Buddha.

Regarding the teaching on transcending stages and kalpas, as stated previously: "Cessation is itself Bodhi. The *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) also states: "To depart from illusion is itself awakening; there is no gradual progression."
All these points share this same meaning.
However, at the time of ultimate awakening, there is likewise no self-result that can be attained; thus, it is said that one "transcends" the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
This is also a designation of "transcendence" based on a comparison of speed—meaning one bypasses certain stages rather than proceeding directly to supreme awakening by skipping all levels entirely.
"This Abhidharma is the single path to Nirvana for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.

Regarding "Abhidharma," it is called the "Incomparable Dharma" (*anuttara-dharma*), which refers precisely to this samādhi; it is also called "Dharma in Confrontation" (*abhidharma*). This means that by means of the Great Equal Wisdom of the Mahāyāna, one confronts the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*), whereby essence and function are manifested and principle and wisdom are of one suchness; therefore, it is named "Dharma in Confrontation."
Bhagavān, he is endowed with six meanings:

"What constitutes fragrance that perfumes my nose?
This is the specific contemplation on the non-arising of fragrance.
Second, the contemplation of benefit.
"By means of this, my mental faculty was dissolved, and I manifested the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The Tathāgata certified me, and I received the name 'Incense Purity' (*Gandhāra*).
Since incense is ultimately without arising, what further discrimination could there be? Therefore, it is said that "the mental faculty was dissolved."

Discrimination does not exist; subject and object are both extinguished. True awakening is unmoving, profound, and eternally pervasive. As defilements have been eliminated, it is perfectly luminous, pure, and wondrous; therefore, it is named "Fragrance Adornment" (Xiangyan).
3. Re-explaining the accomplishment:
"The dust and vapors suddenly vanished, and the wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive; through this 'Array of Fragrance,' I attained Arhatship.
As all marks were exhausted and returned to Suchness, the true fragrance wonderfully emerged; in a single thought-moment of non-discrimination, I ascended to the stage of No-more-learning.
3. Conclusion and Response to the Question:
"Regarding the Buddha’s inquiry into perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the 'Auspiciousness of Fragrance' is supreme.
4. Bhaisajyaraja and Bhaisajyasamudgata, Part Three: [Subdivisions follow]
1. Narrating Past Causes:

The two Dharma-Prince sons of the Buddha, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, along with five hundred Brahmā gods present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“For immeasurable kalpas we have served as excellent physicians for the world. We have tasted every herb, wood, metal, and stone within this Sahā world; there are altogether one hundred and eight thousand such names, all of which we know thoroughly—their bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent tastes—as well as their various combinations, natural properties, and transformations. Whether they are cold or hot, poisonous or non-poisonous, we are able to know them all completely.”
Because he is capable of succeeding to the position of the Regent (Kṣetrapūraṇa) and continuing the lineage of the Buddhas so that it remains unbroken, he is called a "Dharma Prince" (Dharmaputra).
These five hundred Brahmās are his followers; their specific origins are not detailed here.

I recall that in the past, when I served as a physician, I was able to treat various ailments; by tasting medicines, I discerned their flavors and distinguished their natures and functions, ensuring that my treatments were never mistaken.
Having previously mastered the subtle analysis of the sense-object of taste, I have now likewise attained awakening through this very means.
2. Attaining Present Realization, in two parts:
1. Directly Stating the Essence of the Realization:

"Having served the Tathāgata, I have come to understand that the nature of taste is neither empty nor existent; it is neither identical to the body and mind, nor separate from the body and mind. By discerning the cause of taste, I have attained awakening."
"Contemplate from what cause flavor arises: whether it exists within emptiness, the body, or the mind; whether it is identical to them or separate from them—it has no place of origin in any case.
To understand this thoroughly is what is meant by 'observation'."

Because there is no place of arising, the flavors of sensory objects are tranquil; discrimination ceases, and subject and object vanish. Both are utterly devoid of traces, leaving only this single flavor of pure, precious awakening. Therefore it is said that from this one attains enlightenment, which is the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
2. Gaining Benefit through Receiving the Seal.
"We have received the seal of the Buddha-Tathāgata upon the names of us two brothers, the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata; we are now Dharma-princes within this assembly."
"Because they have attained clarity through the faculty of taste, they have ascended to the rank of Bodhisattva.
Since their awakening and enlightenment arose from understanding medicinal flavors, this person is thus sealed as Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
"Ascend" means "to accomplish.
Third, the conclusion responds to the question:
"When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the faculty of taste is supreme."
5. Bhadrapāla (three sections):
1. Awakening through Encountering the Buddha.
Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions, Bodhisattvas, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We previously heard the Dharma from the Buddha King of Majestic Sound and left the household life. While entering the bathhouse according to custom during the time of the monks' bathing, we suddenly realized the cause of water.
Bhadrapāla—also known as Bhadrapāla, meaning "Worthy Protector."
According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, twenty trillion Buddhas named King of Majestic Sound (Prabhūtaratna) appeared in succession.

This person, during the period of the True Dharma of the first Buddha among them, was an arrogant individual who reviled the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging; because of this, he fell into hell and remained there for a thousand kalpas. Once his retribution was exhausted, he emerged and encountered the latter King of Majestic Sound, whereupon he left the household life and attained awakening.
Following the custom, he entered Luoyang and observed that this nature of water was ultimately ungraspable; since it does not arise from causes, he thereby realized the causal nature of water.
Second, the formal presentation of the realization’s purport, in two parts:
first, the narration of the realization and the benefits obtained.

“Neither did he wash away the dust, nor did he wash his body; in the interval, he attained a state of tranquil non-existence. Without forgetting his past habitual tendencies, he has followed me, the Buddha, into the homeless life until now, attaining the stage of No-more-learning.”
Dust has no self-nature; it perishes as soon as it arises.
Its substance is an illusory existence, and its nature and characteristics are fundamentally empty.
Water has no cause and remains peacefully unmoving.
Since all three are non-existent and nothing is attained, what constitutes the act of bathing?
Only when beginningless deluded habits are suddenly extinguished can one now achieve the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Second, a further explanation to confirm this point.
"That Buddha was named I-bhadrapāla; through the manifestation of sublime touch, he became established as a son of the Buddha.

By observing this, once sensory contact with objects has been exhausted, sublime touch manifests before one, and one attains the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), which is called "abiding as a son of the Buddha."
Because he is well able to guard [the mind], causing delusions not to arise and awareness not to waver, he is named Bhadrapāla.
Third, the conclusion that answers the question:
"Regarding the Buddha’s inquiry into perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the cause of touch is supreme."
Because he realized the Way through contact, it is called the "cause of contact.
Sixth, Kāśyapa, three parts:
first, the account of encountering superior conditions, which has three sub-parts:
1. Regarding the Buddha’s reliance on training:
Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Jālinīprabhā, and others rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. I was able to draw near to him, hear the Dharma, and practice it.”
Mahākāśyapa, also known as the Great Kāśyapa of the Piṅgala clan, was named Pipphala. He was foremost among those who practice *dhūta* austerities, and the assembly ranked him as unsurpassed.
Suvarṇaprabhāsā was his wife during their time as householders; the details of their origins are as usual.
First, they shall immediately gain proximity to the Buddhas of Sun, Moon, and Lamp, hearing the Dharma and practicing it.
Second, they shall honor and uphold [the teachings] after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa:
"After the Buddha has passed into extinction, they shall make offerings to his relics, light lamps to maintain the illumination, and gild the Buddha’s images with purple-gold."
"Śrīra means 'the body-bone of the Tathāgata.
The application of oil and gold was all caused by the golden radiance of his body; this has been so throughout successive kalpas and pertains not only to a single Buddha, which is why it is thus."
The sutra provides specific conditions, each according to a single account.
Third, regarding the attainment of results through causes:

"From that time onward, in life after life and birth after birth, my body has always been complete as a mass of purple-gold light; these Bhikṣuṇīs of Purple-Gold Light and the others were my own kinsmen, who simultaneously resolved their minds [for enlightenment]."
As in the text.
Second, the formal presentation of the realization of the ultimate meaning, in two parts:
first, the presentation of contemplative practice.

"I observe that the six sense-objects in the world are subject to decay and transformation; by cultivating cessation through emptiness and stillness alone, my body and mind can pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas as easily as a finger-snap."
The arising and ceasing of the six sense objects is the domain of the mental faculty.

Now, observing these phenomena, they are fundamentally unarisen and presently non-ceasing. Because the mind arises, various phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, various phenomena cease. The mind does not perceive the mind, for no characteristic can be apprehended. Both subject and object are utterly tranquil, and the nature of reality (dharmatā) manifests before one.
Body and mind are fundamentally unmoving; therefore, it is possible to traverse many kalpas in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.
Second, a further explanation for confirmation:

"By means of the dharma of emptiness, I have attained arhatship. The World-Honored One has declared me the foremost among those who practice dhūta, and through the illumination of the wondrous Dharma, all outflows (āsrava) have been extinguished."
Since the phenomena of defilement are empty and the wondrous Dharma is proclaimed and manifested, one attains the state of outflowlessness and achieves the fruit of no-more-learning.
Third, the conclusion that answers the question:
"When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the causal factor of dharmas is supreme."
The above six individuals attained enlightenment by means of sensory objects.
*Śūraṅgama-sūtra-arthavyākhyā-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Five, Part One.
